newsitem.title: USA: U.S. seeks waiver of Georgian diplomat's immunity.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seeks waiver of Georgian diplomat's immunity.

text.p: The U.S. State Department, at the request of U.S. prosecutors, on Tuesday formally asked the former Soviet republic of Georgia to waive immunity so one of its diplomats can be charged in connection with an auto accident last month that killed a 16-year-old girl.

In meetings in Tblisi and Washington, Georgian officials reaffirmed their intention to lift diplomatic immunity for Gueorgui Makharadze, but a formal reply to the U.S. request will take a few days, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said.
"The government of Georgia reaffirmed its intention today to waive Makharadze's diplomatic immunity," Burns said.

But he said, "this is not a formal decision to lift ... we expect a formal reply to the request that we made in Washington and Tblisi in a few days after the government of Georgia has time to digest some of the legal information and explanation of the charges that we conveyed."
Burns said the U.S. Attorney's office, which will prosecute the case, sent a letter on Monday asking the State Department to obtain a formal waiver of Makharadze's diplomatic immunity from Georgia.

On Tuesday, the United States ambassador in Tblisi informed the Georgian government of the specific charges the United States intended to bring against the diplomat. Also on Tuesday a senior State Department official made a similar presentation to the Georgian ambassador in Washington.

Police said speed and alcohol may have played a role in the five-car crash, allegedly triggered when Makharadze, travelling at an estimated 80 miles-per-hour (129 kph), slammed into a car stopped for a red light at Dupont Circle in the heart of Washington.
Prosecutors are expected to seek a grand jury indictment charging him with involuntary manslaughter once Georgia waives his immunity. The charges carry a maximum penalty of up to 30 years in prison.
Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze announced last month he was prepared to lift Makharadze's diplomatic immunity so Makharadze can face charges.
The Jan. 4 accident killed Joviane Waltrick, 16, a Brazilian girl living in Kensington, Maryland.
Newsweek magazine reported that tests at Georgetown University Hospital, taken several hours after the accident, showed Makharadze, 35, had a blood alcohol level far above the legal limit.
Lawyers close to the case said there have been no discussions between prosecutors and Makharadze's attorneys about a possible plea deal.
U.S. Attorney Eric Holder last month wrote to the State Department saying his office believed it had sufficient evidence to prosecute the diplomat if his immunity was waived.
